edits.definition: A High Court is the highest judicial authority of a state, established under Article 214 of the Constitution (one for each state, with some serving two or more states jointly). It hears appeals from the district and subordinate courts in civil and criminal cases, supervises and frames rules for all courts below it, and — like the Supreme Court — can issue the five writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto) to protect the Fundamental Rights of citizens. Its judges are appointed by the President and hold office until sixty-two years of age.

Discrimination is the unfair or prejudicial treatment of individuals or groups on the basis of characteristics that should make no difference to their worth — caste, religion, gender, race, language, disability or economic status. It can be open (denying someone entry, work or schooling) or subtle (paying less for identical work), and it wounds both the person shut out and the society that loses their contribution. The Indian Constitution strikes directly at it: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law, and Articles 15–16 specifically prohibit discrimination by the state on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

Entrepreneurship is the fourth factor of production — the human initiative that brings the other three together. An entrepreneur combines land, labour and capital in the right proportion to run a business, introduces new ideas, products or methods, makes the key decisions about what and how to produce, and takes on the financial risk: if the venture succeeds, the profit is the reward; if it fails, the loss is the entrepreneur's to bear. Without this organizing and risk-taking force, the other factors sit idle — a field untilled, machines unused, workers unhired.

A quadrilateral is a closed plane figure bounded by four line segments called sides, which meet each other only at their endpoints, the four vertices. The figure encloses four interior angles whose sum is always 360°, and its two diagonals join opposite pairs of vertices. The family branches by its sides and angles: trapeziums and parallelograms by parallelism, rectangles, rhombuses and squares by further equalities — so naming a quadrilateral correctly means checking which of these conditions it actually satisfies.

Recording and interpreting observations is the systematic half of any investigation: documenting what is actually seen and measured (qualitative descriptions and quantitative readings) as the experiment runs, organising the numbers into tables and graphs so patterns and anomalies stand out, and then reading those patterns to draw conclusions that answer the original question — accepting, rejecting or refining the hypothesis on the evidence. A result written down late, vaguely or selectively is not evidence; accurate, honest, well-arranged records are what make a conclusion worth trusting.

Justice is the fundamental moral and legal principle that every person is given their due: fairness in procedure, equality before the law, and protection of individual rights, whatever the person's wealth, caste, gender or status. The Indian Constitution names it in the very first line of the Preamble — Justice, social, economic and political — making it not one value among many but the core objective the whole constitutional machine exists to serve, through independent courts, equal laws and rights that any citizen, however humble, may enforce.

Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, experience and health embodied in people that makes their labour productive. It is the qualitative side of the labour force: two workers with the same hours and tools produce very different output if one is trained, healthy and knowledgeable and the other is not. Unlike machines, human capital is built by investment in education, training and healthcare, it grows with use, and its returns — higher earnings, faster growth, better decisions — spread across a whole economy. Spending on a school or a vaccination drive is therefore capital formation in the truest sense.

Urban legacy is the accumulated historical role of cities as engines of economic surplus: from ancient market towns to industrial capitals, cities have concentrated specialised labour, trade networks, stored wealth and public infrastructure in one place, generation after generation. Each era builds on the last — roads upon old trade routes, business districts upon old market squares — so the economic capacity, spatial layout and even the specialisations of a modern metropolis are shaped by what its site has accumulated over centuries. Understanding a city's legacy explains why some urban centres keep outperforming others long after their original advantages have faded.

Shivaji's administration was a centralised yet remarkably lean system of government built in 17th-century Maharashtra. At its head stood the Ashtapradhan — the council of eight ministers (the Peshwa for administration, the Amatya for accounts, the Senapati for the army, and others) — who advised the Chhatrapati and ran their departments, yet held office at his pleasure, without hereditary claims. The land revenue system assessed fields directly and collected a fair share in cash or kind, cutting out the oppressive feudal middlemen; forts, rather than palaces, formed the administrative skeleton of the state, and revenue funded a standing army that moved with the seasons.

Microorganisms, or microbes, are living things too small to be seen with the naked eye — most can be observed only under a microscope. They are grouped into four major categories: bacteria (single-celled, found in soil, water and even inside our bodies), fungi (moulds and yeasts, many made of thread-like filaments), protozoa (single-celled animal-like organisms, some of which cause diseases such as malaria) and certain algae. They exist almost everywhere — in boiling springs, freezing ice, saline flats — and though a few cause disease, the great majority make life on Earth possible: decomposing waste, fixing soil nutrients and fermenting our food.

Uneven resource distribution is the fact that nature's gifts are not spread evenly across the Earth's surface: water concentrates in river basins and monsoon belts, minerals lie where ancient geology put them, fertile soil gathers in plains of old flood deposits, and forests need the right temperature and rainfall. Climate, terrain, altitude and geological history decide these placements, not human choice — no one voted oil under the Gulf or coal under Bihar. The consequence is a world of surpluses and shortages side by side, which drives trade, migration and — where cooperation fails — conflict.

The unique physical features of each continent are the distinctive landforms, water bodies, climate zones and geological structures that set the seven continents apart: Asia's high plateau of Tibet and its Himalayan wall, Africa's Saharan expanse and the Rift Valley, North America's Great Lakes, South America's Amazon and the Andes chain, Australia's desert core and reef coast, Antarctica's kilometre-thick ice sheet, Europe's peninsulas and old low mountains. Tectonic history built the frameworks, latitude fixes the climates, and winds and currents fill in the detail — each continent is a one-off combination of the three.
